Competitive Analysis: Reading the Substitution Structure of a Market

Two product leaders, one in regulated enterprise software and one in connected hardware, discover in the same quarter that their competitor lists were not wrong about the companies — they were wrong about the unit of analysis.

1Two Rooms, Six Weeks Apart

On the morning of 14 August 2026, Meera Vaidyanathan sat in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of Iravati Systems' Gachibowli office in Hyderabad, watching a pipeline review that had been, on its face, reassuring for three consecutive quarters. Iravati sold electronic batch records and deviation management to Indian pharmaceutical formulation plants — the software that turns a plant's paper quality trail into an auditable digital one. The company had closed FY26 at ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue across 61 plants, and the number the chief revenue officer opened with was the one the board liked: in head-to-head evaluations against the large multinational quality-systems vendor that everyone in the room simply called "the global", Iravati had won 20 of 39 contested deals, a 51% head-to-head rate against a company forty times its size. Meera, who had been Iravati's chief product officer for four years and a plant-floor quality engineer for six before that, was looking at a different line on the same sheet. Of 118 qualified opportunities in FY26, only 44 had closed at all. Forty-one — nearly 35% of everything the company had worked — had ended in no decision, against 19% two years earlier. The head-to-head win rate was rising and the business was shrinking. Both facts were true, and the reason they were both true was that the competitor Iravati was beating was not the competitor that was taking its market.

Three weeks later and 1,100 kilometres south, Shalini Bhattacharya faced a narrower-looking question with the same structure underneath it. Shalini ran product at Ilaksh Devices, a Coimbatore manufacturer of commercial-scale water treatment systems — reverse-osmosis and ultraviolet units for hotels, hospitals and food-processing units, each shipped with a telemetry board that streamed membrane pressure, flow and fault codes to a dashboard. The hardware sold well enough: 480 units in FY26 at a list price of ₹4.6 lakh for the 1,000-litre-per-hour model. The attach rate on Ilaksh Assure, the ₹7,500-per-month service and monitoring subscription that carried nearly all of the company's gross margin, had stalled at 38% against a plan of 70%. On 3 September 2026 Shalini was due to recommend whether to fold Assure into the hardware price, and she had discovered while preparing that the answer depended entirely on a question nobody at Ilaksh had asked properly: in a hotel in Jaipur deciding how to get clean water to 120 rooms, what exactly was Ilaksh Assure being compared against? It was not, as the sales deck assumed, a rival manufacturer's telemetry package. It was a local technician with a two-wheeler and a mobile number, who answered in four hours.

Neither of these is a story about missing a competitor. Both companies could name their rivals. They are stories about a subtler and more consequential failure: choosing the wrong unit of analysis. Meera's team analysed vendors when the market was deciding between vendors and self-supply. Shalini's team analysed products when the market was deciding between service response times in a given pin code. This page argues one thing across its length: competitive analysis at an expert level is not the compilation of a list of rivals. It is the estimation of a market's substitution structure — who loses what to whom, under what conditions, at what price, measured in the customer's units rather than yours — and almost every serious error in the discipline is an error in that estimation rather than an omission from the list.

2The Idea, Its History, and the Schools That Disagree

Define the object precisely. A competitor, in the analytically useful sense, is any option whose availability materially reduces the quantity you can sell at a given price, or the price you can charge for a given quantity. That definition is deliberately economic rather than descriptive, and it has three consequences that a list-based definition does not. First, it makes competition a matter of degree rather than membership: two products can be 20% competitive with each other, meaning a fifth of the demand one loses flows to the other. Second, it admits options that are not companies at all — the customer's own staff, a spreadsheet, a maintenance contract, the decision to wait a year. Third, it makes competition segment-specific and occasion-specific: the same two products may compete fiercely in one customer segment and not at all in another, which is why blended competitive assessments so often mislead.

The intellectual history has four strands that modern practice has fused, usually without noticing the seams. The oldest is industrial-organisation economics: Joe Bain and Edward Mason's structure-conduct-performance paradigm in the 1950s, which argued that the profitability available in a market was largely a property of the market's structure rather than of any firm's cleverness. Michael Porter carried that tradition into management in 1979 and 1980, giving managers the five-forces survey and, crucially for our purposes, a definition of industry boundaries that ran through substitution. The second strand is Theodore Levitt's 1960 essay on marketing myopia, which located the boundary not in industry statistics but in the customer's purpose — railroads failed because they defined themselves by the vehicle rather than the outcome. The third strand is the resource-based view — Birger Wernerfelt in 1984, Jay Barney in 1991, Hamel and Prahalad on core competence in 1990 — which insisted that the question "who competes with us" is answered by asking who possesses or can cheaply acquire the resources needed to serve the demand, not by asking who the customer currently considers. The fourth is the demand-side jobs tradition running from Levitt through Clayton Christensen's disruption work in 1997 and the jobs-to-be-done formulations of the 2000s, which supplied the discipline of asking what the customer hired the product to do.

These traditions are not a single consensus with different vocabularies. They disagree, and the disagreements have teeth. The table below sets out five live schools with the specific proposition each would sign and the specific proposition each would refuse, because a practitioner who cannot state the refusals does not really know which school they belong to.

Meera's organisation, without ever debating it, operated on the structural school: it had a defined industry (pharma quality systems in India), a defined rival set (the global, one domestic low-cost vendor, occasional system-integrator custom builds) and a position within it. Shalini's organisation operated on the capability school: Ilaksh's internal argument was that nobody else in India could manufacture the membrane housing and write the telemetry firmware, so nobody else could compete. Both were internally coherent. Both produced a competitor set that excluded the option actually taking their demand — for Iravati, the customer's own IT department armed with general-purpose language models; for Ilaksh, a services relationship that involved no product at all. The empirical school would have caught both, because the empirical school begins not with a list but with a loss.

3Mechanics in Depth: Estimating a Substitution Structure

The expert practice has five moves, of which the middle three are almost never written down. The first move is unremarkable and universally taught: state the customer's job in outcome language without a product noun in it. The last move — choosing a position in response — belongs to a different topic. The three in between are where the discipline actually lives.

Move two: decompose the loss, not the market

Start from demand that did not come to you, and ask where it went. This inverts the usual direction of analysis, and the inversion matters, because a market map built top-down from analyst reports inherits the analyst's category boundaries, while a map built bottom-up from your own losses inherits the customer's. Meera's team, in the last week of August, took all 118 FY26 opportunities and forced every non-win into exactly one destination, verified against a finance record — a signed contract with someone else, a documented internal project, a deferred capex line — rather than a salesperson's recollection.

Figure 1. Loss decomposition for Iravati Systems, FY26. The diversion ratio for each destination is its share of the 74 non-wins. Self-supply at 31.1% is the single largest identifiable destination, larger than the multinational the company had organised its roadmap against.

The quantity in the right-hand column is the diversion ratio, borrowed from merger economics: the fraction of demand lost by product X that goes to option Y. It is the most useful single number in competitive analysis and one of the least used in product organisations, because computing it requires admitting that the largest destination is usually not a vendor. Two properties make it powerful. It is asymmetric — the fraction of Iravati's losses going to the global vendor was 25.7%, while the fraction of the global vendor's Indian losses going to Iravati was, on Iravati's own field estimate, under 4%, because the global vendor lost mostly to price-driven deferral. And it is additive in a way that share is not: diversion ratios tell you what happens to demand at the margin, which is exactly what a price or roadmap decision moves.

Move three: test the boundary with a price experiment

The second implicit move is to stop arguing about who belongs in the market and run the test that economists use to draw market boundaries — the hypothetical monopolist or SSNIP test, adapted. The logic: if you raised price by a small but significant amount and demand did not leave, then whatever you were worried about was not constraining you, and your market is narrower than your competitive deck implies. The arithmetic that makes this operational is critical loss analysis. Critical loss is the percentage of volume you can afford to lose from a price rise before the rise stops being profitable, and it is given by

Critical loss = Δp ÷ (Δp + m), where Δp is the percentage price increase and m is the contribution margin as a percentage of price.

Iravati's contribution margin is 78%. For an 8% price rise, critical loss = 8 ÷ (8 + 78) = 9.30%. In other words, if Iravati raised renewal pricing 8% and lost fewer than 9.3% of the affected revenue, the increase paid for itself and the "competitive pressure" the sales team invoked every renewal season was not, at that margin, real. Meera ran exactly this as a controlled test across 30 renewals in the first quarter of FY27: two accounts, representing 6.7% of the affected revenue, refused and churned. Actual loss below critical loss. The conclusion was not "we should raise prices" — that is a pricing decision with other considerations — but something more analytically important: at the renewal stage, Iravati faced almost no substitution. Once a plant's batch records were validated inside Iravati's system, the alternatives were prohibitively costly. At the acquisition stage, by contrast, substitution was overwhelming: 55% of new demand went to no decision. Iravati was operating in two different competitive structures simultaneously, and its single competitive analysis, blended across both, described neither.

Move four: score the entrants who are not yet competing

The third implicit move is forward-looking and is where the resource-based school earns its place. A competitor set assembled from observed diversion is by construction a description of the past. The correction is to score adjacent players on two dimensions and to make the second dimension quantitative. The first is capability distance: how much an adjacent firm would have to build, buy or validate to serve your customer's job. The second is incentive to enter, which can be estimated as a payback period on bundling. Meera's team worked this for the global vendor: adding a lightweight batch-record module to its Indian offering would cost roughly ₹9 crore of build and ₹2.4 crore a year to support; the vendor's Indian base of about ₹265 crore might see churn improve 1.5 percentage points, worth ₹3.98 crore a year, for a net ₹1.58 crore against a ₹9 crore build — a payback of about 5.7 years. Large vendors do not fund 5.7-year paybacks in a secondary geography. The same arithmetic for Ishaanvi Labs, a Pune startup selling an AI agent that drafts deviation investigations from a plant's existing documents, produced a payback under nine months, because its marginal cost of covering an additional document type was close to zero. The conclusion was counter-intuitive and correct: the company Iravati feared would not enter, and the company it had never heard of could not afford not to.

Payback periods are computed from build cost, incremental support cost and estimated retention or revenue gain; a payback longer than a typical planning horizon is strong evidence of non-entry, and a payback shorter than a sales cycle is strong evidence of imminent entry.

The second-order effects of doing this work are worth naming, because they are what separates a useful practice from a performative one. Publishing an internal competitor list changes behaviour: teams optimise against what is measured, so a list circulated widely becomes a roadmap by stealth, and the roadmap converges with the rival's. Convergence, in turn, shifts the basis of competition to price, which favours whoever has the lower cost of capital — usually not you. A second effect is the survivorship bias in sales-sourced intelligence: field teams only report on deals they were invited into, so the intelligence system systematically under-observes the customers who never ran an evaluation at all, who are precisely the self-supply segment. A third is reflexive: naming a rival publicly recruits their attention and gives their sales team a free comparison to run. Mature organisations therefore separate the analytical map, which must include self-supply and inertia, from the enablement map, which is what field teams see, and they accept that the two are different documents with different audiences.

4When the Discipline Applies, and When It Actively Misleads

The conditions under which competitive analysis produces reliable guidance can be stated as five testable claims. Stating them as claims matters, because each can be checked against a specific observation rather than asserted.

Claim one: substitution is observable in behaviour. The test is whether you can obtain a defensible diversion estimate — a documented destination for at least 70% of lost demand. Iravati passed: 74 of 74 non-wins were assigned a finance-verified destination. Ilaksh failed initially and this was the root of its trouble: 480 units sold told the company nothing about the 1,100 quotations that did not convert, because Ilaksh's dealers, who issued the quotations, had no obligation to record why. Where this claim fails, everything downstream is guesswork dressed as analysis, and the first investment must be in loss instrumentation rather than in strategy.

Claim two: the job is stable over the analysis horizon. The test is whether the outcome the customer wants has been described in the same words by customers three years apart. Iravati fails this test in an interesting way: the job "produce an auditable quality record" has been stable for decades, but the cost of producing it without software collapsed in 2025-26, so the job's economics moved even though its description did not. That is the most dangerous variant of instability, because the standard sanity check does not catch it. Shalini's job — "guests and inspectors never encounter a water problem, and I do not add headcount" — has been stable and remains so.

Claim three: the customer chooses. Competitive analysis assumes a chooser weighing options. Where a third party constrains the choice set — a hospital formulary, a government empanelment list, a retailer's shelf, a regulator's approval, a parent company's global vendor agreement — the binding contest is for inclusion in the list, not for preference within it. Roughly a fifth of Iravati's addressable plants belong to groups whose global parent mandates a vendor; for those, competitive analysis of product merit is simply the wrong exercise.

Claim four: the option set is enumerable. This is the claim that AI-native markets break. When the substitute is "a competent person with a general-purpose model and three weeks," there is no firm to name, no pricing page to monitor and no product to benchmark. The set is not enumerable; it is a capability distribution across your customers' own staff. The analysis must change shape, from a list to a cost curve — what does it cost the customer to self-supply, and is that cost falling faster than your price?

Claim five: your cost structure is comparable to theirs. Where a rival serves the job as a by-product of something else it already does, its marginal cost may be near zero and no amount of product superiority will close the gap. Ilaksh faces this against the local AMC technician, whose marginal cost of adding a water unit to an existing hotel maintenance round is an hour of travel he was making anyway.

There are also situations where the discipline is not merely uninformative but actively harmful. The first is a genuinely new category with no diversion data: here competitive analysis will confidently report that your only competitor is inertia, which is true but useless, and the far more valuable exercise is demand validation. The second is when the binding constraint is supply rather than demand — a diagnostics chain competing for radiologists, a marketplace competing for delivery riders, a services firm competing for engineers. Competitive analysis aimed at customers in those situations analyses the wrong market entirely. The third is the imitation trap the category-design school warns of: in markets where differentiation is the only route to margin, a rigorous competitive map handed to an engineering organisation reliably produces a roadmap that is the union of competitors' features, which is the most expensive way to become average.

5Hard Edge Cases and the Organisational Seams

Multi-product portfolios. A company with five products has two competitive positions that can point in opposite directions: product-level competition against best-of-breed specialists, and account-level competition against other portfolios. The specialist beats each module; the portfolio beats the sum, because the buyer values one contract, one integration and one throat to choke. The seam appears when product managers, incentivised on their module's win rate, lobby for features that beat the specialist, while the account economics say the right move is deeper cross-product integration that no single module's scorecard rewards. Mature companies handle this by running two scorecards and being explicit about which one governs a given investment, rather than by pretending one exists.

Two-sided markets. The analysis must be run twice and joined at the multi-homing rate. The side that single-homes is the scarce side and sets the competitive dynamic; the side that multi-homes experiences little switching cost and generates deceptive loyalty data. A freight marketplace that shows 80% shipper retention and 30% truck-operator retention is not an 80% business — the operators are the constraint, and the operators' true competitor is a direct relationship with the shipper that disintermediates the platform entirely.

Regulated markets. Regulation does three things to a competitive set and practitioners routinely notice only the first. It excludes entrants (a licence requirement). It creates demand on a schedule, which converts the "do nothing" option from a permanent alternative into a timing decision — India's revised Schedule M requirements for pharmaceutical manufacturing, phased for smaller units, did exactly this for Iravati, replacing "never" with "by a deadline". And, least noticed, it standardises the product so heavily that differentiation migrates to implementation, validation and service, where the competitor is a consultancy rather than a software firm.

Hardware plus software. Three specific distortions. First, the installed base is a competitor to the new product: Ilaksh's biggest obstacle in FY26 was Ilaksh units installed in 2021 that still worked. Second, the aftermarket has its own competitive structure — grey-market membranes at 40% of Ilaksh's price, sold by the same technicians who service the units. Third, and most consequential, service geography partitions the market: Ilaksh won 58% of contested deals in the 11 cities where it employed its own technicians and 22% in the 34 cities served by franchise partners, where mean time to restore was 31 hours against six. A national competitive assessment is a weighted average of two entirely different competitive positions, and the average describes no city.

AI-native products. Four things break at once. The model provider is simultaneously supplier, distributor and potential competitor. Differentiation built on a model's current limitation has a half-life set by someone else's release schedule — the capability-overhang problem, where a feature representing eighteen months of your engineering is absorbed into a base model and becomes free. The customer's self-supply cost falls continuously rather than stepwise, so the diversion ratio toward self-supply drifts upward without any competitor action. And evaluation becomes probabilistic: buyers compare outputs on their own data, so the competitive contest happens inside a pilot you cannot observe or control.

The organisational seams. In most companies, competitive intelligence is owned by product marketing, loss data by sales operations, pricing by finance, and roadmap by product — four owners, four instruments, no shared denominator. The characteristic failure is not ignorance but non-reconciliation: sales' battlecards name three rivals, finance's churn analysis attributes losses to price, and product's roadmap assumes feature gaps. What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what they describe in their operating manuals, is narrower and more boring than the textbook: a single quarterly loss review with finance-verified destinations for every non-win above a revenue threshold; one named owner per material rival, held responsible for a one-page constraint assessment rather than a feature comparison; and a standing register of "conditions that would change our view", each with a monitoring owner. The elaborate competitive portals get built, and then they go stale within two quarters because nobody's incentive depends on them.

6Ten Nuances That Separate the Expert from the Competent

Overlap is not competition; diversion is. Two products can share 90% of their feature surface and compete for nothing, because they serve different segments, geographies or buying centres. The tell-tale sign an expert looks for is a rival that appears constantly in market maps and almost never in your own win-loss records — high perceived overlap, near-zero measured diversion. The obvious reading, that you are simply not being invited into those deals, is occasionally right and usually wrong; the more common truth is that the two products stopped competing some time ago and the map has not caught up. Acting on overlap rather than diversion produces roadmap investment aimed at a rival who is not taking your customers.

The no-decision bucket is three different rivals wearing one label. "No decision" conflates not now (budget timing), not this way (the customer will self-supply) and not a problem (the job is not painful enough). These require opposite responses: the first is a pipeline-timing issue, the second is a genuine competitor requiring a pricing or packaging answer, the third is a segmentation error requiring you to stop selling to those customers. The tell-tale sign is a no-decision rate that is high and undifferentiated in the CRM. Iravati's 41 no-decisions split 23 / 11 / 7 across these three, and the single most valuable analytical act of Meera's quarter was insisting on that split.

Your field team's competitor list is a survivorship sample. Sales sees the deals it was invited into. Customers who never ran an evaluation — who decided in a corridor conversation to keep doing what they were doing — are invisible to the system that generates most competitive intelligence. The tell-tale sign is a competitor list whose composition is stable while the ratio of qualified opportunities to addressable accounts is falling. The obvious reading, that the market is saturating, is wrong more often than it is right; the usual truth is that a substitute has become good enough that evaluations no longer get run.

Substitution shows up in price before it shows up in share. A new alternative first appears as a discount you had to give, then as a longer sales cycle, then as lost deals, then as lost share — in that order, often over six to nine months. The tell-tale sign is realised average selling price drifting down while win rate holds. Teams read stable win rate as evidence of stable competitive position; it is in fact the last indicator to move, and a practitioner who watches only win rate learns about substitution two quarters after their pricing already told them.

The most dangerous competitor usually starts as a complement. The sequence is reliable: a firm integrates with you, learns the workflow, observes which parts carry margin, and absorbs those parts. The tell-tale sign is a partner whose integration traffic is growing much faster than the revenue it refers — they are learning more than they are selling. The obvious reading, that a growing integration is evidence of a healthy partnership, is exactly backwards when the partner controls the customer relationship and you control only a replaceable step.

Competitive relationships are asymmetric, and asymmetry makes behaviour unpredictable. If you represent 0.7% of a rival's revenue, as Iravati did of the global vendor's, they will not respond to you globally and may respond savagely locally, because the local general manager's bonus is at stake even when the corporation's strategy is indifferent. The tell-tale sign is aggressive discounting in your market accompanied by no product response — a local reaction without corporate backing. Expecting symmetric attention is the error; the practical consequence is that you should model your rival's decision-maker's incentives, not the rival's.

Feature parity is a tax, and the expert distinguishes reasons-to-reject from reasons-to-choose. Some capabilities never win a deal but can lose one: audit-trail exports, single sign-on, a regional data-residency statement. Others genuinely drive selection. The tell-tale sign of a reason-to-reject is a capability that appears in every RFP and in no win-reason interview. Treating those two classes identically is what produces the me-too roadmap the category-design school condemns; treating them differently lets you spend the minimum on hygiene and concentrate the rest on the one or two dimensions that actually move choice.

A rival's constraints predict better than their roadmap. Roadmaps are aspiration and marketing; constraints are physics. Where is the rival hiring, in what functions and cities? What has changed on their pricing page? What is their support SLA, and does it imply staffing they cannot afford? What does their channel margin have to be for dealers to carry them? The tell-tale sign of a constraint-bound competitor is loud announcements paired with unchanged hiring. The obvious reading — that an announced product is a threat — should be discounted heavily until the constraint evidence agrees.

Share of the job is denominated in the customer's budget line and labour hours, not in your category's revenue pool. Iravati's category, on analyst definitions, was worth a few hundred crore in India. The budget line it actually drew from — quality documentation labour across the same plants — was several times larger, and that is the pool self-supply was drawing from too. The tell-tale sign that you are using the wrong denominator is a total addressable market computed by multiplying a category size by a share ambition. The right denominator is what the customer currently spends, in money and in hours, to get the outcome by any means.

Category membership is a distribution asset, not a truth claim. Experts hold two positions at once without embarrassment: the job-true view, which governs what they build and where they expect substitution, and the category-pragmatic view, which governs how they describe themselves so that budget, analyst coverage and procurement templates can find them. The tell-tale sign of a practitioner who has not internalised this is either a company that describes itself in a category it cannot win, or one that insists on a novel category label and then cannot be found in any buyer's shortlist. The obvious reading — that you should describe yourself as what you truly are — ignores that buyers search using the vocabulary of the budget they hold.

7How the Practice Differs by Product Type and Stage

Some of these differences are real and some are asserted, and it is worth separating them. In consumer products the competitor set is wide and attention-denominated; substitution is fast, cheap and frequently reversible, so diversion ratios are measurable in weeks and worth measuring often. In B2B and enterprise, the set is narrower but the buying centre is plural, and the single most important structural difference is that the person who states the evaluation criteria is usually not the person who chooses between self-supply and purchase. A competitive analysis conducted only with users will systematically under-weight the build option, because building is never the user's budget. This is not a nuance; it is the difference between Iravati's FY24 analysis and its FY26 one.

For platforms and marketplaces, as discussed, the analysis must be run per side and joined at the multi-homing rate; the scarce side governs. For hardware and physical goods, geography partitions the market via service and distribution, the installed base competes with the new product, and the aftermarket is a separate competitive arena with its own participants. For AI products, the enumerable-set assumption fails and the analysis becomes a cost-curve comparison against self-supply, revisited far more often than any other product type would require.

Where the differences are not real is worth stating plainly, because a great deal of ink is spent asserting them. The mechanics of loss decomposition are identical across all five types — you find where demand went and you verify it. Critical loss analysis works the same for a subscription and for a consumable. The distinction between reasons-to-reject and reasons-to-choose applies as cleanly to a hotel's water system as to an enterprise platform. And the tendency of competitive analysis to degenerate into a feature race is universal; nothing about being consumer or enterprise, hardware or AI, protects an organisation from it.

Stage changes emphasis more than method. A pre-product-market-fit company should spend most of its competitive effort on the self-supply and inertia options, because the central risk is that the job is not painful enough to be hired for. A scaling company should invest in loss instrumentation, since it is generating enough losses for diversion estimates to become statistically meaningful — this is the stage at which the discipline pays the highest return and is most often neglected in favour of growth mechanics. A mature company already knows its rivals and should shift effort to segment-level analysis and to the adjacency map, because its characteristic failure is not ignorance of competitors but a blended view that conceals a reversal in one segment. Iravati, at ₹96 crore, was exactly at the transition and was still running the pre-fit playbook of tracking named rivals.

8Three Worked Examples, Including One That Failed

Example one: the segment reversal hiding inside a blended win rate

Iravati's 37.3% overall win rate concealed three different businesses. In injectables plants, where regulatory scrutiny is highest and the cost of a quality failure is measured in export revenue, Iravati won 20 of 33 contested opportunities — 61%. In oral solids, 18 of 62 — 29%. In active-ingredient and intermediates plants, 6 of 23 — 26%. The blended number, 37.3%, was not a description of any of them. More importantly, the no-decision rate ran the other way: 12% in injectables, 41% in oral solids, 48% in API. The interpretation follows directly. Where the cost of a quality failure is high, self-supply is unattractive because nobody wants to explain a homemade system to an inspector, and Iravati competes against vendors and wins. Where the cost of failure is lower, self-supply is rational and Iravati competes against the customer's own IT team and loses. Two different competitive structures, one company, one scorecard. The correct response was not a better product but a different commercial motion in the two segments — and the recognition that in one of them Iravati's competitor was a build-versus-buy calculation, which is won on total cost of ownership and risk transfer, not on features.

Example two: the crossover volume that decided which rival mattered

Shalini's team costed the job — "reliable potable water for a property" — over a year, for a 120-room hotel, across the four options a general manager actually considers. The exercise required pulling costs the sales deck had never shown: amortised capital, consumables, power, service, and the cost of downtime estimated from guest-compensation records.

The competitive position was not a property of the product; it was a property of volume and of pin code.

Example three: the analysis that was rigorous and wrong

In FY24 Iravati had done the textbook exercise properly. It ran 40 structured interviews with quality-assurance heads at target plants, derived weighted selection criteria by pairwise comparison, scored itself and the global vendor against them, and found one dominant gap: depth of validation documentation, weighted at 0.34 of the decision. The company committed ₹6.2 crore and fourteen months of its engineering capacity to closing that gap. The project succeeded on its own terms. Head-to-head win rate against the global vendor rose from 38% to 51% over the following two years — the very number the board was applauding in August 2026. And over the same period, average contract value fell 19% and the no-decision rate climbed from 19% to 35%.

The failure was not in the method's execution but in a single unexamined choice: whom to interview. Quality-assurance heads are users and often the loudest voice in an evaluation, but they do not hold the budget, and the option "we build something ourselves" never occurs to them because it is not their project to run. By eliciting criteria only from users, Iravati constructed a scorecard in which self-supply could not appear as an option, and then invested ₹6.2 crore optimising against the competitor that scorecard did contain. The analysis was internally rigorous and structurally blind. The recovery, which Meera began in September 2026, had three parts. First, criteria were re-elicited from the whole buying centre with influence weights — quality head 0.35, plant head 0.25, plant IT 0.25, finance 0.15 — which immediately surfaced build-versus-buy as the dominant axis for 0.40 of the decision weight. Second, the company built a deliberate cost-curve comparison against self-supply rather than against vendors: what does a plant spend to build and validate its own system, and what does it spend to keep it validated as regulations change? The second half of that question turned out to be Iravati's real advantage, since a self-built system must be re-validated by the plant every time a requirement moves, at an estimated ₹34 lakh and four months per cycle. Third, Iravati introduced a ₹19 lakh entry tier aimed squarely at the self-supply decision rather than at the global vendor's ₹64 lakh price point, accepting the margin dilution as the cost of competing in the contest that was actually happening. The cost of catching the error late was not only the ₹6.2 crore; it was fourteen months of engineering capacity spent moving a number that measured the wrong contest, during which Ishaanvi Labs went from nothing to 22 plants.

9Failure Modes, Their Early Warnings and the Cost of Late Detection

Mirror-imaging. Assuming a rival optimises what you optimise. The early warning is a competitive assessment that predicts a rival's behaviour and is repeatedly wrong in the same direction. The diagnostic question: what is this competitor's decision-maker compensated on, and what would they have to give up to do what we expect? Caught late, the cost is a defensive investment against a move the rival was never going to make.

Competitor-driven roadmaps. The roadmap becomes the union of rivals' feature sets. The early warning is a roadmap in which most items can be traced to a competitor's release note rather than to a customer outcome. Diagnostic: for each of the next five roadmap items, which specific loss does this reverse, and what was the diversion ratio of that destination? Caught late, the cost is two to three years of convergence, after which differentiation must be rebuilt from a worse position and price has already fallen.

The blended number. Reporting one win rate, one score, one market. The early warning is a competitive metric that moves smoothly quarter to quarter while segment-level results diverge. Diagnostic: split the number by the three variables most likely to matter — segment, deal size, and geography or service coverage — and check whether the ranking of competitors reverses in any cell. Caught late, the cost is investment aimed at the average of two markets, which serves neither, as Ilaksh's national pricing did.

Eliciting criteria from the wrong role. Discussed above at length. The early warning is a criteria list containing no cost-of-ownership or risk-transfer items, which is the signature of a user-only panel. Diagnostic: which of our evaluation criteria would a chief financial officer recognise as theirs? Caught late, the cost is a large, well-executed investment in the wrong dimension — Iravati's ₹6.2 crore.

Intelligence theatre. A handsome competitive portal, battlecards refreshed quarterly, and no decision anywhere in the company that has ever been changed by them. The early warning is that no one can name a decision the last four quarters of competitive intelligence altered. Diagnostic: show me the last roadmap item, pricing change or segment exit that this system caused. Caught late, the cost is mostly the opportunity cost of the analysts, plus a false sense of coverage that delays the real analysis.

Defining the threat away. "They're downmarket." "That's a toy." "Those aren't real deployments." The early warning is a rival dismissed with a category argument rather than a numerical one, twice in successive quarters. Diagnostic: what is their diversion ratio this quarter against last, and in which segment? Caught late, this is the most expensive failure in the catalogue, because by the time a dismissed entrant is undeniable it has usually acquired the reference customers that make the next hundred sales easy.

Confusing the acquisition contest with the renewal contest. The early warning is a single competitive narrative used in both new-business and renewal conversations. Diagnostic: run the critical-loss test on renewals; if actual loss is well under critical loss, you are not facing meaningful substitution at renewal and should stop discounting as if you were. Caught late, the cost is silent and continuous — margin given away on renewals to a competitive threat that does not exist in that context, which was costing Iravati an estimated ₹3 to 4 crore a year in unnecessary renewal concessions.

10Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Map the competition or escape it. The category-design position, in its strongest form, is not that competitive analysis is inaccurate but that it is organisationally corrosive: the act of measuring yourself against rivals installs their choices as your agenda, and since the analysis is easier to act on than differentiation is, organisations drift toward imitation regardless of what the strategy document says. The evidence is the observable convergence of mature software categories and the reliability with which benchmark-driven roadmaps precede price competition. The opposing position holds that escape is a fantasy without a map — that you cannot know which dimensions are unoccupied without knowing which are occupied, and that most "category creation" is retrospective narrative applied to a company that in fact won a conventional contest. For the first position to be wrong, we would need cases where rigorous competitive mapping reliably preceded genuine differentiation rather than imitation; for the second to be wrong, we would need a meaningful set of winners who demonstrably never did the mapping. Both bodies of evidence are thinner than the confidence of their advocates.

Revealed versus stated preference. The empirical camp holds that only behaviour counts: diversion ratios, price tests, switching data. Its strongest argument is that stated criteria are systematically distorted — buyers under-report price sensitivity and over-report feature rationality — and that Iravati's FY24 failure is a textbook demonstration. The interview-based camp responds that revealed preference can only describe options that were on the table, and is therefore structurally blind to demand that never became a transaction, which is exactly the self-supply segment that the empirical camp claims to be best at finding. For the empirical position to be wrong, we would need markets where the decisive alternative never appears in any observable transaction; those exist, which is the honest state of the argument.

Is "doing nothing" a competitor or a market condition? One camp insists inertia is the largest rival and must sit in the competitive set. The other holds that treating inertia as a competitor is a category error that invites the wrong response — you cannot take share from inertia by product comparison, only by changing the cost or urgency of the job, which is a demand-creation problem, not a competitive one. The practical stakes are real: the first framing sends you to build; the second sends you to marketing, pricing or segment exit. No serious practitioner disputes that inertia matters; they dispute which instrument it belongs to.

What AI does to substitution structure. One position: AI collapses the cost of self-supply and therefore permanently raises the diversion ratio toward building, making software differentiation shallower and shifting durable advantage to data, distribution and workflow ownership. The counter-position: self-supply has always looked cheap at the prototype stage and expensive at the maintenance stage, and AI lowers the cost of the first without touching the second, so the apparent shift is a repeat of the 1990s spreadsheet-versus-system argument that vendors won. Iravati's own data cuts both ways — 23 plants did build, and Meera's team estimated re-validation at ₹34 lakh per regulatory cycle, which is exactly the maintenance cost the counter-position predicts will bring them back. Whether it does is, at the time of writing, genuinely unknown, and any page that tells you otherwise is selling something.

11What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied competitive analysis produces a competitor list, a feature matrix and a positioning statement, refreshed quarterly and presented well. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways. They begin from losses rather than from markets, and they refuse to accept a loss reason that a finance record cannot corroborate. They speak in diversion ratios and cost curves rather than in rival names, and when asked "who is our biggest competitor" they answer with a segment and a percentage rather than a company. They maintain two documents, not one — the analytical map that contains self-supply and inertia, and the field enablement map that does not — and they are untroubled by the difference. They watch their own realised price as a leading indicator of substitution, not their win rate. They score potential entrants by payback period rather than by plausibility, which lets them ignore frightening rivals with slow economics and take seriously unfrightening ones with fast economics. And, most distinguishing, they know which claims their analysis rests on and check them: when someone at Iravati now proposes a competitive conclusion, the first question is whether the option set is enumerable and whether the customer is actually the chooser — because if either claim fails, the conclusion is not weakly supported, it is inapplicable.

There is a seventh behaviour that is harder to describe and easier to recognise: mastery shows up as restraint. The expert does not add rivals to the watch list because they appeared in a news article, does not commission a study when a price test would answer the question in six weeks, and does not let a competitive finding become a roadmap item without first asking which measured loss it reverses. The competent practitioner's competitive deck grows every quarter. The expert's gets shorter and more numerical.

12What They Decided

Meera presented on 30 September 2026. She did not open with competitors. She opened with the diversion decomposition of Figure 1 and the observation that the company had spent fourteen months and ₹6.2 crore improving its performance against the destination that absorbed 25.7% of lost demand while ignoring the one that absorbed 31.1%. Her recommendations were three. Iravati would stop investing in feature parity against the global vendor, whose 5.7-year bundling payback made it a slow rather than an urgent threat, and would explicitly accept losing some injectables deals on documentation depth. It would launch the ₹19 lakh entry tier positioned against self-supply, with the commercial argument built on re-validation cost across regulatory cycles rather than on features. And it would instrument loss properly: finance-verified destinations for every non-win, a quarterly critical-loss test on renewal pricing, and a standing adjacency review scored by payback period. The board's hardest question was the one Meera had least evidence for: whether Ishaanvi Labs, with a nine-month payback on scope expansion, would reach a full quality system before Iravati reached the self-supply segment. She said honestly that she did not know, and that the decision was a bet on regulatory validation being harder to cross than product scope.

Shalini presented on 8 October, having withdrawn her original recommendation. She did not bundle Assure into the hardware price. Instead she proposed three changes that followed from the crossover arithmetic. Ilaksh would stop quoting properties consuming under 250 litres a day, where jarred water genuinely wins and where the dealer network had been losing two thirds of its quotations and calling it a price problem. It would sell Assure only in territories where a contractual mean time to restore under eight hours was achievable, which meant 11 cities immediately and a defined expansion sequence, rather than nationally at a price that assumed a service level Ilaksh could not deliver. And it would stop treating the local AMC technician as a rival to be displaced and start enrolling that network as a certified channel, paid on uptime rather than on parts — converting the competitor with the lowest marginal cost into the distribution the company lacked. The dissent in the room was serious and unresolved: the sales director argued that ceding sub-250-litre properties surrendered the volume that made the factory efficient, and he was not obviously wrong.

Discussion questions.
  1. Iravati's head-to-head win rate against the global vendor rose from 38% to 51% while its business deteriorated. Under what circumstances is a rising head-to-head win rate evidence of strategic health, and what additional measurement would you require before treating it as such?
  2. Shalini proposes to enrol the local AMC technicians — the option with the lowest marginal cost of serving the job — as a certified channel. What does this do to Ilaksh's competitive position in five years, and under what conditions does co-opting a substitute become handing it your market?
  3. Meera's recovery rests on the claim that regulatory re-validation cost will pull self-supplying plants back to a vendor. State the evidence that would confirm or refute this within twelve months, and decide what Iravati should do differently if the evidence has not arrived by then.

13Going Deeper

The product strategy document
Competition is one section of it; the discipline here is what makes that section falsifiable rather than decorative, and it constrains every other section's claims.
Positioning
Having established who you actually compete with, positioning is the deliberate choice of which comparison to invite and which to refuse — the direct downstream decision from a diversion map.
Five forces and industry structure
Supplies the supply-side and bargaining-power analysis this page deliberately set aside, and explains why some markets are unprofitable for everyone regardless of competitive skill.
Competitive response and war-gaming
Turns a static map into a dynamic one by modelling what rivals do after your move — essential once your action is large enough to provoke a reaction.
Competitive intelligence practice
The operational machinery: sourcing, ethics, cadence, and how to build a loss-instrumentation system that survives contact with a sales organisation's incentives.
Competing on the job, not the category
Develops the demand-side school in full, including how to elicit a job statement that does not smuggle your product's shape into the question.
Private label and retailer competition
The sharpest real-world case of a channel partner becoming a competitor, with the bundling economics worked out in a market where the rival also controls your shelf.
Competing with local incumbents abroad
Shows how competitive sets change with geography and regulation — the same product faces a different structure in each market, as Ilaksh's pin-code effect previews.
Right to win
Forces the honest question this analysis raises but does not answer: in which of these contests do we have an asymmetric advantage, and in which are we merely present?
Moats and the 7 Powers
Classifies the durable advantages that determine whether a favourable competitive position persists after rivals respond intelligently.
Network effects
The mechanism that makes diversion ratios self-reinforcing, and the main reason a small early share difference can become unrecoverable.
Switching costs and lock-in
Explains Iravati's asymmetry between acquisition and renewal directly, and how to measure lock-in rather than assume it.
Moats in the AI era
Takes up the unresolved disagreement in section 10 about whether falling self-supply costs permanently raise substitution.
Counter-positioning
The strategy of adopting a position the incumbent cannot copy without damaging its existing business — the most reliable escape from the parity race described here.

Iravati Systems, Ilaksh Devices and Ishaanvi Labs are fictional companies constructed for teaching purposes; their figures are illustrative. References to Indian pharmaceutical manufacturing regulation, packaged-water economics and hospitality operations are used as factual market context only. Academic works cited are real and are attributed to their authors.

Competitive Analysis: Who Is Actually Taking Your Customer's Job?

Aruna Kapoor had built the best expense-tracking app in her category. The board wanted to know why a bank with no category ambitions was winning anyway.

1The Tuesday the Category Stopped Mattering

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Aruna Kapoor stood in front of Anshika Money's board in a conference room on the eleventh floor of a Lower Parel tower and watched a slide do more damage than any competitor ever had. The slide was simple: monthly active users, flat for the fourth straight quarter at 4.1 lakh, against a target the board had approved eighteen months earlier of 9 lakh. Aruna was Anshika Money's VP of Product, and for three years the company's pitch had been clean and, she had believed, correct: young, salaried Indians needed a dedicated app to see where their money went, set savings goals, and split bills with roommates and friends without the friction of a spreadsheet. Anshika Money did that job well. Independent app-store reviews rated its auto-categorization among the best in its segment, its UI had won a design mention in a fintech trade publication, and churn among users who stayed past ninety days was a respectable 4% a month.

The problem, as the board's newest independent director put it without much diplomacy, was that Anshika Money's rivals list — the one Aruna had presented every quarter for three years — named four other standalone budgeting apps, and none of them had grown either. The market for dedicated budgeting apps, as a category, had stalled. Meanwhile a neobank called Advait Pay, which had never once described itself as a budgeting tool, had quietly shipped free automatic spend categorization inside its core UPI and savings-account app, bundled at no extra cost, and had absorbed an estimated 1.8 million users who fit Anshika Money's exact target profile in the same eighteen months. Advait Pay's product team had never benchmarked itself against Anshika Money. It didn't need to. It had simply made Anshika Money's core job — see where the money goes — a free feature of something people already used for something else. Aruna's stated competitors had not touched her numbers. An unstated one had gutted them. She had six weeks before the next board meeting to tell the room, credibly, who Anshika Money was actually competing with, and what to do about it — and she knew that if she got the diagnosis wrong a second time, the conversation would no longer be about strategy but about whether the company had a reason to exist.

2The Idea, Defined Precisely

Competitive analysis is the disciplined, evidence-based practice of identifying every organization, product, workaround, or non-action that a customer could reasonably use to get a given job done at least as well as your offering does — and weighing them against each other by the value each actually delivers against that job, rather than by how similar each looks to you on the surface. The phrase sounds like common sense, which is exactly why it is so often done badly: most product teams quietly narrow "competitor" to mean "other companies that describe themselves the way we describe ourselves," and that narrowing is the single most common strategic error a product organization makes, because customers do not organize their choices by category label. They organize their choices by outcome.

The intellectual lineage of this idea runs through two distinct traditions that modern practice has fused. The first is Theodore Levitt's 1960 Harvard Business Review essay "Marketing Myopia," which argued that American railroads had nearly destroyed themselves by believing they were in the railroad business rather than the transportation business, and had therefore failed to notice trucks, cars, and airplanes as competitors until those substitutes had already taken the customer's job away. Levitt's contribution was the insight itself: define your business, and therefore your competition, by the customer need served, not by the technology or format you happen to use to serve it. The second tradition is more structural: Michael Porter's 1979 Harvard Business Review article "How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy," later expanded into his 1980 book Competitive Strategy, which gave managers a systematic way to survey an industry's boundaries — rivals, new entrants, substitutes, and the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers — rather than relying on instinct about who felt like a threat. Competitive analysis as it is practiced today borrows Levitt's discipline of defining the job broadly and Porter's discipline of surveying systematically, and adds a habit product organizations have developed since: explicitly including "the customer does nothing, or keeps doing what they already do" as a competitor in its own right, because inertia beats almost every launch in its first year. The sentence Aruna could say in that boardroom without sounding glib was this one: "We compete with everyone who can deliver the outcome our customer wants, including the option of doing nothing, and we have only been counting the ones who look like us."

Figure 1. The concentric map: the job at the centre, direct competitors in the inner ring, substitutes and alternatives in the outer ring, and inertia as the outermost — and usually largest — rival. Anshika Money had only ever mapped the inner ring.

3How the Mapping Actually Gets Done

Competitive analysis, done properly, is a sequence of steps, and the steps most teams skip are the ones that require the most intellectual honesty rather than the most research effort. The first step is to write down the customer's job in plain, outcome-based language, deliberately stripped of any product noun — not "an app for tracking expenses" but "know, without effort, where my money went and whether I am on track," which is the version of the job a customer would state to a friend, not to a vendor. Aruna's team had, in fact, never written this sentence down; their internal documents described the product as "a budgeting and bill-splitting app," which is a description of a product, not of a job, and it had quietly restricted three years of competitive scanning to other things called budgeting apps.

The second step is to list every way a real customer currently gets that job done, sorted into three honest tiers rather than one flattering one: direct competitors, who solve the same job with a recognizably similar approach (other budgeting apps); alternatives and substitutes, who solve the same job through a different mechanism, often as a byproduct of something else the customer was already doing (a neobank's bundled categorization, a UPI app's spend summary, a credit card statement's category breakdown); and the default, meaning what the customer does if no product exists at all — manual mental tracking, a notebook, a spreadsheet, or simply not knowing and not minding. The third step is to resist ranking these tiers by market size or brand recognition and instead rank them by the actual share of the job each currently captures among the target customer — a number that usually has to be estimated from user interviews, support tickets, and win-loss conversations with churned users, because no research firm publishes it. The fourth step, the one practitioners most often leave implicit, is to separate "who competes with us today" from "who is one product decision away from competing with us" — Advait Pay did not exist as a threat to Anshika Money in its own founding pitch deck; it became one the day its product team decided categorization was cheap to bundle. A competitive map drawn once a year misses exactly this kind of entrant, because the entrant was never a company Aruna's team had reason to watch — it was a company that changed its scope.

The fifth step is to evaluate every competitor, including the default of doing nothing, on the same small set of weighted criteria that actually drive the customer's choice, rather than on a generic feature checklist — this is the mechanism the worked example below walks through in full. The sixth and final step is to revisit the weights themselves periodically, because the criteria that matter to a customer shift with the news cycle, with regulation, and with what has just gone wrong for someone they know; a competitive analysis that never re-weights its own criteria is describing a market that no longer exists.

4A Worked Example: Scoring the Real Field

Aruna's team ran the analysis the way it should have been run from the start. They defined the job as above, listed four contenders that customers actually used to do that job — Anshika Money itself; Advait Pay, the neobank; a plain spreadsheet; and doing nothing, meaning informal mental tracking — and, through twenty-two structured interviews with recent switchers and twelve with loyal spreadsheet users, derived five criteria that customers said actually drove their choice, along with the relative weight each criterion carried in a typical decision. The weights had to sum to 1.00, and the team used a simple pairwise comparison exercise with the interview panel to set them: automation (how little manual work the option required) carried the most weight at 0.30, followed by trust and data security at 0.25, cost to the user at 0.15, social and bill-splitting features at 0.15, and habit-forming nudges at 0.15. Each option was then scored from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion by the research team, based on interview evidence and direct product testing, and each score was multiplied by its criterion's weight to produce a weighted total out of 5.

Anshika Money's total is built as (0.30 × 4) + (0.25 × 3) + (0.15 × 4) + (0.15 × 5) + (0.15 × 4) = 1.20 + 0.75 + 0.60 + 0.75 + 0.60 = 3.90. The gap is narrow — a tenth of a point on a five-point scale — but it is a gap in the wrong direction, and it is a gap driven almost entirely by the two heaviest-weighted criteria, automation and trust, where a bundled neobank has structural advantages a standalone tracking app cannot easily match: it already holds the transaction data natively, and it already holds the trust relationship that comes with being the account of record. The second pass is what makes the tool genuinely useful rather than a one-time snapshot. Three weeks after this first scoring exercise, the Reserve Bank of India published a fresh advisory tightening data-sharing disclosures for consumer finance apps, following a widely covered breach at an unrelated fintech lender — a reminder that trust in Indian fintech was, in late 2026, a live and moving variable rather than a fixed one. Aruna's team re-ran the interview panel's pairwise weighting after the news cycle and found trust and security had risen to 0.35 of the decision, automation had fallen to 0.20 as users grew slightly more suspicious of frictionless auto-linking, and the other three weights held at 0.15 each. Recomputed, Anshika Money's total became (0.20 × 4) + (0.35 × 3) + (0.15 × 4) + (0.15 × 5) + (0.15 × 4) = 0.80 + 1.05 + 0.60 + 0.75 + 0.60 = 3.80. Advait Pay's became (0.20 × 5) + (0.35 × 4) + (0.15 × 5) + (0.15 × 2) + (0.15 × 3) = 1.00 + 1.40 + 0.75 + 0.30 + 0.45 = 3.90. Advait Pay still led, but the spreadsheet — scored 5 on trust throughout, because it touches no third party at all — climbed from 2.75 to (0.20 × 1) + (0.35 × 5) + (0.15 × 5) + (0.15 × 1) + (0.15 × 2) = 0.20 + 1.75 + 0.75 + 0.15 + 0.30 = 3.15, closing nearly a full point of the gap to Anshika Money in three weeks without a single product change on the spreadsheet's part. That is the lesson a single scoring exercise cannot teach and a re-weighted one can: your competitors' scores can move even when your competitors do nothing at all, because the criteria themselves are not fixed.

Figure 2. The second pass: nobody changed their product, but a shift in what customers weighed most moved every score. Anshika Money's lead over the spreadsheet nearly halved without a single competitor lifting a finger.

5Eight Nuances a Learner Must Hold in Mind

Category and job are not the same map, and conflating them is the single most common error

A category is how companies describe themselves to investors and journalists; a job is what the customer is actually trying to get done. Two products can sit in entirely different categories — a neobank and a budgeting app — while competing intensely for the same job, and two products can share a category label while barely competing at all if they serve different jobs within it. Always draw the competitive map from the job outward, never from the category inward.

Scope of "the job" is a judgment call, and drawing it too wide is its own failure mode

Define the job too narrowly ("track categorized expenses in an app") and you miss Advait Pay entirely, as Aruna's team did for three years. Define it too widely ("help people with their finances") and everything from a mutual fund to a life-insurance agent becomes a "competitor," which dilutes the analysis into uselessness. The test is whether a real customer, in their own words, would describe two options as solving the same immediate problem on the same afternoon — that is usually the right altitude.

Competitive analysis is not the same exercise as a feature comparison chart

A feature checklist counts what a product has; competitive analysis weighs what the customer values and how well each option, including doing nothing, delivers against that weighting. A product can lead every row of a feature chart and still be losing, exactly as Anshika Money was, because the features it leads on are not the ones carrying the decision's weight.

"Doing nothing" is not a null category — it is frequently the largest single competitor

New-to-category products routinely underestimate inertia because inertia has no logo, no funding round, and no press coverage to track. In Aruna's own data, doing nothing and the spreadsheet together represented a larger share of the addressable job than either funded competitor. Ignoring the default because it is hard to research is a bias, not an analytical shortcut.

Weights are not permanent facts about the market — they are current facts about the customer's mood

As the second pass showed, a single regulatory advisory moved the ranking of every competitor without any competitor changing its product. A competitive analysis performed once a year and then treated as settled is quietly describing a market that has already moved on. Re-score at least when a major exogenous event plausibly changes what customers care about, not only on a fixed calendar.

An adjacent player's decision to enter can convert a non-competitor into a category-defining one overnight

Advait Pay was never a competitor by Anshika Money's original definition; it became one the day its product team decided bundled categorization was cheap to ship. Competitive analysis has to include a forward-looking layer — who could enter this job cheaply given what they already have — not only a backward-looking survey of who currently competes.

Scores are estimates built from interviews and testing, not measured facts, and the method must be disclosed alongside the number

A weighted total of 3.90 looks precise; it is in fact a structured aggregation of twenty-two switcher interviews, twelve loyalist interviews, and a research team's product testing, each carrying its own margin of error. Presenting the number without the method invites false confidence in the boardroom — and, just as dangerously, invites the next team to treat last quarter's scores as this quarter's truth.

Competitive analysis tells you where you stand; it does not tell you what to build

The scorecard told Aruna precisely where Anshika Money was losing and why — but it did not, by itself, tell her whether to chase automation and trust on Advait Pay's terms, retreat to a defensible niche around social features, or exit the standalone-app format altogether and seek a distribution partnership. That decision belongs to positioning and to strategic choice, both of which sit downstream of this analysis, not inside it.

6How the Picture Changes by Product Type and Stage

In consumer products like Anshika Money, competitive analysis has to reach unusually far outward, because consumer attention is fungible across categories in a way B2B budgets rarely are — a consumer's "budgeting job" competes not only with other finance apps but with anything that reduces their anxiety about money, including a habit as low-tech as checking a bank SMS. In B2B products, the competitor set is typically narrower but the default of "doing nothing" is far stronger and far more rational, because an enterprise buyer switching tools incurs procurement cycles, training costs, and integration risk that a consumer downloading a free app does not; a B2B competitive analysis therefore has to weight switching cost far more heavily than a consumer one does, and frequently finds that the true rival is not a competing vendor at all but the incumbent spreadsheet or legacy system the buyer has already paid to integrate. In marketplace products, the analysis has to be run twice, once for each side of the market — a ride-hailing marketplace competes for riders against other apps and against owning a vehicle, and separately competes for drivers against other platforms and against salaried employment, and a map that only scores one side will misread half the business.

Stage changes the exercise as much as product type does. An early-stage company, still searching for product-market fit, benefits most from mapping the full breadth of alternatives and the default, because the central risk at that stage is building a better version of something nobody was choosing to begin with — better than a rival that itself never had traction. A large, established company benefits more from depth than breadth: it usually already knows its major rivals, and the analytical value shifts toward re-weighting criteria frequently, watching for adjacent entrants the way Anshika Money failed to watch for Advait Pay, and running the scorecard by customer segment rather than as one blended market-wide number, since a large company's user base is rarely one job any longer but several.

7Common Mistakes

The first common mistake is category myopia: defining competitors by who else uses the same product noun, which is precisely the error that cost Aruna three quarters. The symptom is a competitor list that has not changed in over a year even as growth has stalled; the underlying misunderstanding is treating the category label as the unit of competition instead of the customer's job; the cheapest diagnostic is to ask ten recent churned users, in their own words, what they switched to, and count how many answers are not on the official competitor list.

The second common mistake is feature-checklist thinking: building a comparison grid of features present or absent, then concluding superiority from a higher checkmark count. The symptom is a team that feels confident about its competitive position on paper while losing share in the market; the underlying misunderstanding is scoring what the product has rather than what the customer weighs; the cheapest diagnostic is to ask the same ten churned users to rank, unprompted, the three things that mattered most in their decision, and compare that ranking to the features the internal chart emphasizes.

The third common mistake is treating the scorecard as permanent rather than as a snapshot of a specific moment's weights. The symptom is a competitive deck that looks unchanged from one board meeting to the next even after a visible market event; the underlying misunderstanding is mistaking a competitive analysis for a one-time deliverable instead of a living instrument; the cheapest diagnostic is to check the date the weights were last revisited against the date of the most recent relevant market or regulatory event.

The fourth common mistake is ignoring the default option because it is unglamorous and hard to research, which quietly inflates every funded competitor's apparent share of the real contest. The symptom is a competitive map with no "doing nothing" row at all; the underlying misunderstanding is assuming that a job without a product against it must be a small job; the cheapest diagnostic is a single question in every churn and win-loss interview — "if none of these products existed, what would you actually do?" — and a genuine count of how often the honest answer is nothing.

8What Good Looks Like

Six weeks later, in the same eleventh-floor conference room, Aruna returned to the board with a different kind of slide. She did not open with a competitor list; she opened with the job definition, stated in one sentence a customer might actually say, and then showed the concentric map and the weighted scorecard, both passes, side by side, with the method — interview counts, scoring basis, the date of the last re-weighting — written in small type beneath each. She named Advait Pay explicitly as the structural threat it was, explained in plain arithmetic why its bundled advantage sat on the two heaviest-weighted criteria, and did not pretend the news was better than it was. What made the presentation land was not the discovery of a new threat; every board member in the room had, in some informal way, already sensed Advait Pay's rise. What landed was that Aruna could now show precisely how much of the gap was structural (automation and trust, hard to close quickly) versus how much was addressable (habit-forming nudges, where Anshika Money's own weighted score of 4 already beat Advait Pay's 3), and she used that distinction to propose a specific, narrower positioning — leading with social bill-splitting and habit design for shared households, a job Advait Pay's individual-account architecture could not easily replicate — rather than a vague commitment to "compete harder." Good competitive analysis, done well, does not produce comfort. It produces a map precise enough that the next decision follows from the evidence rather than from the loudest voice in the room.

9What Aruna Decided, and Two Questions Worth Sitting With

Aruna recommended, and the board approved, a repositioning of Anshika Money away from general budgeting — the job it was structurally weakest to win against a bundled neobank — and toward shared-household money coordination, the job its scorecard showed it was already winning on the criteria that mattered to that narrower segment. She also proposed a standing quarterly re-weighting of the scorecard rather than an annual one, triggered additionally by any material regulatory or trust event in Indian fintech, so that the next Advait Pay would be visible as an adjacent entrant before it had absorbed two million users rather than after. The next topic worth studying, once this one is comfortable, is positioning: having mapped who you truly compete with and on what customers value, the next discipline is choosing, deliberately, which of those values you will own outright and which you will concede — because a company that tries to lead on every criterion in the scorecard usually leads on none of them, as Anshika Money's own middling trust score against a neobank's home-field advantage had just demonstrated. Two questions are worth sitting with before moving on. First: when you last mapped your own competitors, did the exercise start from the product category your company uses in its own pitch deck, or from a sentence a real customer would use to describe the job, stated without any product noun in it at all? Second: which of your current criteria weights would most embarrass you if you had to defend, out loud, when they were last revisited — and what event, already visible in the news, should have triggered a re-weighting that has not yet happened?

Sit with these:

1. When you last mapped your competitors, did you start from your own category label or from the customer's job stated without a product noun?

2. Which of your scorecard's weights are most out of date — and what already-visible event should have triggered a re-weighting?

Anshika Money and Advait Pay are fictional companies constructed for this case. Reference to the Reserve Bank of India, real UPI-linked apps, and named publications is used only as factual market context.

The Counter and the Cashbox

Competitive analysis at Rasoi Counter Systems, Indore — September 2026

1. Sunday night, Mumbai

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 27 September 2026, Nandita Apte sat on the floor of a hotel room in Bandra Kurla Complex with three printed exhibits spread across the carpet. She was co-founder and Chief Product Officer of Rasoi Counter Systems, the Indore company whose software ran the billing counters of 21,500 restaurant outlets, and in ten hours she had to name to her board the one thing Rasoi would build in FY27.

The three sheets did not agree. One said Rasoi was losing to Rangoli Kitchen Cloud, the Bengaluru firm giving restaurant software away free since September 2025 and now claiming 31,000 outlets. One said it was losing to Lipi Billing Systems, the twenty-two-year-old Coimbatore company that still sold a perpetual desktop licence and turned up in more Rasoi deals than anyone. The third, in from Toronto at 7.40, said most leavers used no restaurant software at all.

Sameer Kulkarni had texted at ten: Board wants one slide. One bet. Not a landscape. She replied that she was not sure Rasoi knew who it was losing to. He did not answer.

2. How Rasoi got here

Rasoi was founded in 2016 by Sameer Kulkarni, whose family ran a sweet shop in Indore's Sarafa Bazaar, and Nandita Apte, who had built point-of-sale software in Pune. Their premise was correct: mid-market Indian restaurants wanted a counter that worked when the broadband did not and cost less than a waiter.

The decision that still shapes everything was taken in 2019. To break Lipi's hold on tier-two cities — Indore, Nagpur, Coimbatore, Ludhiana, Ranchi — Rasoi matched Lipi's model instead of attacking it, selling an offline-first Windows product on a perpetual licence at ₹42,000 one time with an optional ₹9,000 annual maintenance contract. It placed 6,800 in fourteen months and won the reference density everything afterwards rested on.

Two legacies followed. The first is legal: those 6,800 outlets can be neither repriced nor force-migrated, and yield ₹9,000 each against a blended ₹51,372. The second is architectural. The 2019 engine holds each outlet's menu, prices and day-book in a local database on the counter machine; the 2021 cloud product inherited the schema, so a chain's head office is nowhere a first-class object. Anirudh Kamat, who runs engineering from Bengaluru, has told the board that a real multi-outlet console — one menu, one price list, one royalty statement across 148 outlets — is a rewrite of the transaction core.

In March 2023 Rohtang Growth Partners led a ₹310 crore Series B at ₹1,680 crore post-money, with a covenant nobody argued about: if net revenue retention fell below 100 per cent in any year, Rasoi would need investor consent for any tier priced below ₹12,000 per outlet a year. FY26 retention was 97.7 per cent.
