3. The industry

Indian food-service software runs on three economics and Rasoi competes with all of them without having decided which it is. The first is licensed software — Rasoi's model and Lipi's — where the restaurant pays; Petpooja and Restroworks sit beside Rasoi in those bake-offs. The second is platform software: Zomato and Swiggy give marketplace partners a dashboard, reporting and payout reconciliation free, because the software is a cost of acquiring order flow. The third Rasoi has been slowest to name — software as an acquisition channel for payments and credit. Rangoli charges nothing for its counter application and earns on settlement and on advances against card receivables.

Beneath all three runs UPI. A dynamic QR from PhonePe, Paytm or BharatPe and a ₹2,000 soundbox give an owner digital collection, a settlement record and spoken confirmation of every payment with no counter software at all; ONDC now offers direct orders outside the marketplaces. Regulation cuts both ways: GST e-invoicing and FSSAI licence display push small outlets towards some system, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has turned the diner phone numbers in Rasoi's loyalty module from a free asset into a consent liability.

Of 21,500 outlets, 1,450 are in the Gulf, where Indian-cuisine groups run large franchise estates and UAE e-invoicing is forcing operators to revisit their systems, and 850 are in North America. Those two geographies are 10.7 per cent of outlets and 32.1 per cent of revenue.

  1. Using Exhibits 1, 3 and 5, sort Rasoi's competition into direct competitors, alternatives, substitutes and doing nothing. Which categories does Rasoi's reporting capture, and which are invisible by construction?

  3. Exhibit 5 shows Rasoi winning 70 per cent against Lipi and 45 per cent against Rangoli. Which is the more dangerous competitor — and what does the last row do to your answer?
  4. Two-thirds of churned outlets produced a third of churned revenue, and one account most of the large-chain loss. Is Laziz a pattern or an anecdote, and how should a product leader weigh one large data point?
  5. Exhibit 6 compares a software business with what may be a lending business. If Rangoli's column is broadly right, is Rasoi's problem a product gap, a pricing gap or a business-model gap — and does any option address the third?
  6. It is Monday morning. Nandita has one slide, 34 engineer-quarters, a covenant, a Dubai RFP due in eighteen days and two datasets that contradict. What goes on the slide, what does she say when Akhil Vora asks why she passed over the best return per engineer-quarter, and what does she tell the board she still does not know?

At half past midnight she laid Exhibit 3 over Exhibit 5 and held both up to the lamp. What she kept returning to was a line in the calling vendor's transcript: an owner in Bhopal, asked what he used now, had said he used his son. The boy sat at the counter with a phone, took the UPI payment, wrote the order in a notebook and added it up at eleven at night. He had not chosen Rangoli or Lipi. He had looked at ₹36,000 a year and decided what Rasoi sold was worth less than a notebook and a boy who was home anyway.

Rasoi had lost 3,780 of those last year, or 1,058, depending on which sheet she believed. In nine hours she would have to say which.
case20v1-comp.analysis:
Who Are We Really Losing To?

Competitive analysis at Chahat Rewards Cloud, Pune — September 2026

1. The scene

On the morning of Tuesday, 22 September 2026, Kabir Anand, VP Product at Chahat Rewards Cloud, sat in the company's Kalyani Nagar office in Pune with two spreadsheets open and three weeks to make sense of them. On 14 October he was due to present the FY27 product roadmap to the board that had approved Chahat's Series B eighteen months earlier on the promise that it would become the default employee-recognition layer for Indian corporates. Engineering had capacity for exactly one major build before the next funding conversation, so the slide had to name one bet, not three.

The urgency had a sharper edge. Chaman Facilities Group LLC, a Dubai-headquartered facilities-management group with roughly 3,800 India- and UAE-based staff on Chahat's platform and its largest single account, had a renewal decision due by 31 October. Its India HR director had told Priyanka Nair, Chahat's Singapore-based customer success lead, that engagement had "gone quiet" and that the group was evaluating a bank-issued cashback card instead. Kabir needed a roadmap that answered two questions together: what should Chahat build for FY27, and was Chaman's complaint a one-off or a symptom of something larger.

2. Company background

Chahat Rewards Cloud sells a SaaS platform that lets HR teams recognise employees with points, badges and milestone awards redeemable across a curated marketplace of vouchers, experiences and merchandise. Founded in 2018, it serves 240 enterprise and mid-market clients across manufacturing, IT services, BFSI and retail, for FY26 annual recurring revenue of ₹84 crore — an average contract value of ₹35 lakh per client.1 Engineering sits mostly in Bengaluru and Pune and product design out of Berlin. HR buyers routinely shortlist Chahat against real Indian players selling the same points-and-marketplace model — Vantage Circle, Advantage Club and Xoxoday's Empuls — and board decks had always named these three as "the competition."

What the decks had not shown, until Meher Chawla, Chahat's Toronto-based head of data and insights, ran a proper win-loss study, was how small a share of lost deals those three names actually accounted for.

3. The situation

Between January and June 2026 (Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27), Chahat's sales team logged 50 competitive RFPs that reached proposal stage and did not convert. Meher's analysis, in Exhibit 2, sorted each loss by what the client actually chose — not by who the account executive assumed they had lost to. Fourteen losses went to another points-and-marketplace platform: Chamak People Rewards, a Chennai rival undercutting on price, or one of the three real incumbents. Twenty-one losses, the largest bucket, went to something that was not a recognition platform at all: a bank-issued, Zaggle-powered prepaid card crediting a monthly cashback allowance straight to an employee's account, sold by HR as a "flexible benefit" rather than a "reward." Nine losses went to a plain increase in the cash-bonus line, processed through ordinary payroll tools such as RazorpayX Payroll with no dedicated software at all. The remaining six clients simply kept their existing manual, Excel-and-gift-voucher process and approved no new spend.

Chaman's complaint fit the second bucket, not the first. Its HR director was not comparing Chahat to Chamak; she was comparing the ritual of logging in to redeem points against a card that puts money in an account with no login at all. Sanjay Mehta, Chahat's New Jersey-based head of sales, saw the same pattern across his North American and Gulf pipeline and argued that the twenty-one-deal bucket, not the Chaman account alone, was the real FY27 problem. Priyanka, closest to the one client actually walking, wanted an answer she could give Chaman before 31 October.

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is simple: before deciding what to build, decide who you are actually competing with. Product teams default to comparing themselves against companies that look like them — Chahat's own decks, before Meher's study, named only Chamak People Rewards and the three real incumbents. That undercounts the competition, because a buyer's budget does not care what shape a solution takes; it cares what job gets done. A cashback card and a points marketplace both draw on the same "make employees feel rewarded" line, even though one has a login screen and the other has none.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. First, it uses Exhibit 2 to separate direct competitors (same solution shape, same budget) from alternatives (different mechanism, same job — the cashback card), substitutes (a cruder fix for the same need — a bigger bonus), and doing nothing (the true default, understated at 12% since most non-buyers never issue an RFP at all). Second, it weighs the single Chaman anecdote against the aggregate pattern and finds they agree: Chaman is not an outlier, it is the largest account sitting inside the largest loss bucket. Third, it sizes the response by the number, not the anecdote, using Exhibit 4.

On that basis, Option B is the defensible path. It is the most expensive and slowest of the three, and a board member fixated on return per rupee could reasonably favour Option C's 5.3x (₹3.20 crore on ₹0.60 crore) over Option B's 1.3x. But return on build cost answers the wrong question: the issue is not which bet is cheapest to justify but which competitor is taking Chahat's revenue. Option A defends 28% of the problem; Option C, a sound second-order move for FY28, defends 12% of it among buyers who never appear in the loss log. Option B alone is sized to the 42% bucket that dominates the data and sits under Chahat's largest client. Kabir's recommendation should be Option B, paired with a low-cost commitment to keep the Chaman relationship warm through October — not because the anecdote demanded it, but because the arithmetic did.
